explanation: Fires on digits or words inside a large monetary or physical quantity, especially the token right before a magnitude word like 'billion', 'million', 'trillion', 'crore', 'sq ft' (e.g. '$2[4] billion', 'hundreds[ of] millions'). Plain percentages and measurements without a big-magnitude word give only weak to moderate activation.

No clear concept. Fires on a mix of code tokens (require paths, import statements, ' The' in copyright headers), broken non-Latin multibyte characters, and function words in idioms like 'on[ the] path/verge' and 'do[ the] same'.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a long technical or medical word that is split into pieces (e.g. 'demodex[fol]liculorum', '[spl]enic', 'metap[las]ia', '[clar]ifiers', 'anthelm[int]ic'), mostly in scientific or patent text. Also fires on some ordinary words partway through a phrase ('our[ own]', 'in[ their]'). Whole common words give weak activation.

Fires on the first fragment of a word split into subword pieces, especially word-initial 'lo', 'rep', 'P', 'ap' (e.g. '[lo]oting', '[rep]atriated', '[P]roud', '[AP]PELLATE'), in many languages and in code. Whole-word tokens are weak.

Fires on a token that begins a new name or noun phrase after a setup context, often the first fragment of a proper name or acronym ('[D]DT', '[G]abbard', '[O]ta', '(MET)') or a content noun ('header[ files]', 'her[ fingers]'). Activation is spread across many kinds of context and has no single clear trigger.

Fires on joining tokens inside lists or compound expressions: the operator between function terms in algebra ('-5*j(s)[ -] 2*p(s)'), the comma after a patent application number before 'filed', 'and' between two named entities, and similar continuation points. Also fires on some role nouns ('writer'). Fairly mixed.

Fires on the second token of fixed tech or boilerplate phrases: 'using namespace[ std]', 'source[ code]', 'PL/[SQL]', 'OS[ X]', 'Crypto.Public[Key]', 'at the[ very] least', 'commercial[ use]'. The preceding word predicts the token, which completes a familiar collocation.
Mixed. Fires on 'PER CURI[AM]' in court opinions, on cookie-related tokens in JS code, on sentence adverbs ('Not[ surprisingly]', 'willingly'), and on assorted word completions. No shared concept.

Fires on the preposition 'of' or 'to' right after a relational noun that takes a complement: strongest for 'presence[ of]', 'access[ to]', 'capability/capabilities[ to/of]', also 'entitled[ to]', 'remember[ to]', 'wealth[ of]'. Prepositions after other words are weak.

Fires on the later subword piece of a word or name split into tokens ('cl[ank]', 'cod[ility]', 'cloud[front]', 'K[im]berling', 'msg[str]', 'Stack[ Overflow]'), across code, names and onomatopoeia. Has no semantic theme.

Fires where a number or ordinal is expected: the second '-' in 'a - -b' arithmetic, counting/ordinal words like 'second[ season]', 'final[ quarter]', 'three straight', citation index digits ('[@B[4]]'), and numbers in ranges. Broadly about numbers, counts and sequence positions, with some noise.

Fires on words about aesthetic style, character or authenticity, mostly in music, fashion and design text: 'style', 'personality', 'authentic', 'sound', 'accent', 'Revival', 'unapologetically', Vietnamese 'phong cách'. Strongest when the word describes someone's distinctive manner or look.

Fires mainly in copyright/license header boilerplate: the period after the holder name before 'All Rights Reserved', the word 'reserved', and 'License' in 'under the License'. Also fires on some code delimiters and trailing zeros in timestamps.

Fires on the first fragment of a word split into subword tokens, especially 'br' ('[br]icked', '[br]aced', '[br]ash'), 'l', 'ab', 'fl', 'Ham', 'Ses'. The token is word-initial and the rest of the word follows in later tokens.

Mixed. Fires on HTTP header or option key names in code ('Authorization', 'Cookie', 'HttpMethod', 'step'), on medical subword pieces ('macro[ph]ages', 'endosc[op]ically'), and on 'to'/'with' in phrases like 'according[ to]', 'brought[ to] you'.

Mixed bag: citation brackets '[@', question openers ('What'), domain suffixes ('.biz', 'Kos'), spread operators, and various adjectives and verbs ('inspected', 'indispensable', 'unfit'). No common thread.

Mostly fires in software license boilerplate: the period in 'Boost Software License, Version 1.0[.]', 'furnished[ to] do so', 'WARRANTIES[,]'. Also fires on assorted prepositions and nouns in ordinary prose ('in', 'for', 'services'), which share nothing obvious.

Fires on digits inside citation and DOI identifiers (e.g. '[@B1-ijerph-17-0[1]067]', 'JAHA.1[1]7'), plus a scatter of unrelated tokens in prose and code ('Robert', 'cheated[ on]', 'system[ path]'). Citation-ID digits are the main reliable trigger.

Mixed: the period or comma after judge names and case captions in legal documents ('Circuit Judges[.\n]', 'District Judge'), digits in chemical names and citation IDs, medical subwords, and assorted prose words. No unifying concept.
Fires very strongly on 'pone' in PLoS ONE citation keys ('[@pone.0...'). Weaker activations on assorted tokens at sentence or paragraph starts ('.\n\n', 'According', 'Let'), which look unrelated.

Fires on the number two in any form: '2', 'two', 'iki', 'both', 'dual', 'bi-', and less strongly 'second'. Strongest when it counts items ('I have [2] classes', 'divided into[ two] groups'). Years and version numbers containing 2 are weak.
